figures.caption: Neutrophil accumulation is increased across multiple organs in aged mice. (A) Schematic overview of scRNA‐seq sampling of multiple organs from young and aged mice. (B, C) t‐SNE plots of integrated scRNA‐seq data from multiple organs, colored by tissue origins (B) or annotated cell types (C). Boxes indicate the interquartile range, center lines indicate the median, and whiskers extend to 1.5 × the interquartile range. (E–H) Immunofluorescence of indicated tissues in young and old mice. Green: CD11b, Purple: MPO, Blue: DAPI. Scale bars are shown in the picture. Data are shown as the mean ± s.e.m., *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01; ***p < 0.001. Wilcox rank sum test was used in (D), and t‐test was used in (E–I).

figures.label: FIGURE 2
figures.caption: Neutrophils from aged mice display enhanced inflammatory and effector‐associated programs. (A) t‐SNE plot of the integrated neutrophil atlas from multiple organs, including blood, intestine, liver, lung, vascular tissue, heart, kidney, and brain, colored by age group. The number of neutrophils contributed by each group is shown in the accompanying bar plot. (B) Volcano plot showing differential gene expression in neutrophils from aged versus young mice. Genes with adjusted p value < 0.05 and log2 Fold Change > 0.5 were designated as differentially expressed genes. (C, D) Hallmark functional enrichment analysis of gene sets enriched in neutrophils from aged (C) or young (D) samples. Dot size represents gene count and color indicates adjusted significance. (E) Sample‐level comparison of marrow proximity and reactive oxygen species (ROS) module scores in neutrophils from young and aged mice. Each dot represents one biological sample. (F) Representative Cytox Green staining images showing NET formation in neutrophils isolated from young and aged mice. Quantification of NET‐positive cells is shown on the right, each data point represents one biological replicate. Scale bar, 50 μm. (G) Representative senescence‐associated β‐galactosidase (β‐Gal) staining images of MOVAS and AML‐12 cells following treatment with conditional medium derived from young or aged neutrophils. Quantification of β‐Gal‐positive cells is shown on the right, each data point represents one biological replicate. Scale bar, 20 μm. (H, I) Immunoblot (H) and its quantification analysis (I) of MMP12, MMP9, P16, and P21 expression in MOVAS and AML‐12 cells treated with conditioned medium from young or aged neutrophils. GAPDH served as a loading control. Relative protein intensities normalized to young group are indicated below each blot. Each plot represents an independent biological replicate. (J) Relative RNA expression of senescence‐associated secretory phenotype (SASP) genes (Il6, Tnf, and Ifn) and extracellular matrix remodeling genes (Mmp3 and Mmp9) in MOVAS cells following treatment with conditioned medium from young or aged neutrophils. Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m. Statistical significance was determined using two‐sided unpaired t‐test (E–G, I) and two‐way ANOVA followed by Tukey's multiple‐comparisons test (J). *p < 0.05; **p < 0.01; ***p < 0.001.

ai.summary_zh: 该论文提出LSTM-EWMA筛选与分派框架:将有序基因组区域表示为特征向量序列,用仅在预设受控(IC)区域上训练的LSTM建模基线模式,并对标准化预测残差施加EWMA控制图;超出预设控制限的区域被操作性地标记为失控(OC),作为下游软件推荐候选,未标记区域保留默认处理路径。作者强调这些标签仅描述计算工作流状态,不单独确认变异或生物学异常。基于人类参考基因组合成测序数据的初步方法学基准中,该方法在评估设置下区分了预设OC与IC区域并保持较低观测误报率。图注显示评估仅区分基线调用器窗口(code 1)与路由至下游推荐流程的窗口(codes 2–5),codes 2–5间的选择不在本次评估范围内。
learning_points: 将基因组区域序列化为特征向量序列,用LSTM建模仅受控区域的基线模式,再对标准化预测残差使用EWMA控制图进行异常筛选。
采用“筛选—分派”两阶段思路:仅对超限区域触发下游软件推荐,以降低逐区域上下文感知推荐的计算开销。
明确标签语义边界:OC/IC标签表示计算工作流状态,不独立确认基因组变异或生物学异常。
图1界定了评估范围:仅区分基线调用器窗口(code 1)与下游推荐候选窗口(codes 2–5),候选间选择属下游阶段、不在本次评估内。
图2以描述性控制图对比ARIMA–EWMA、LSTM+固定阈值与LSTM–EWMA,背景色标识五类参考调用器类别,红色标记表示报警。
图3、图4分别对λ与窗口大小做单次运行敏感性分析,指标为FPR、F1-score与检测延迟。
代码静态观察显示run_experiments.py以header=None读取CSV,并保存基线对比、性能表、λ/窗口敏感性、ROC与消融等图件;作者代码未运行,静态检查不构成复现验证。
论文将当前结果定位为模拟数据上的可行性初步基准,并指出需在微生物、宏基因组及宿主关联测序情境中进一步验证。

figures.caption: Disturbed serine metabolism occurs in nucleus pulposus cells (NPCs) during senescence. GO analysis revealed significant enrichment in cell cycle‐related pathways (I), whereas KEGG analysis highlighted prominent enrichment in the glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism pathway (J). K, L Volcano plots of DEGs showing that phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH), the rate‐limiting enzyme for serine synthesis, was downregulated in both group B and group C compared with group A. figures.caption: The latent causal diffusion (LCD) model and CLIPR. (A) LCDs model single-cell expression data y (Top) as noisy observations of unobserved, noiseless gene states x (Center). States x are samples from a stationary stochastic process x(t) evolving under the causal regulatory dynamics f(x) of an SDE (Bottom). To train LCDs, we first infer p(x) via empirical Bayes, then learn f in state space via score matching. (B) Dynamics f explicitly model gene regulation and are parameterized by a neural network with shared hidden state across genes. Perturbations modify this hidden state via learned embeddings eq. (C) To interpret the causal dependencies in f, we estimate a linear causal matrix that induces the perturbation behavior of f (Left). This matrix is computed from the initial (vfq) and limit (ℓfq) responses when f is perturbed. The limit response is approximated by following the vector field flow until convergence (Right).
figures.attribution: Lars Lorch; Jiaqi Zhang; Charlotte Bunne; Andreas Krause; Bernhard Schölkopf; Caroline Uhler. Latent causal diffusions for single-cell perturbation modeling.. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2602630123. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.

figures.label: Fig. 2.
figures.caption: LCDs outperform state-of-the-art models at predicting combinatorial perturbation effects. (A) Maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between predicted and observed single-cell expressions for held-out double-gene perturbations of the two datasets, computed on top 20 differentially expressed (DE) genes. Each dot represents one perturbation. Two leftmost bars show baseline performance of randomly sampled control and perturbed cells from all conditions. (B) Per-perturbation comparison of LCD with deep-learning baselines on MMD, normalized to [0,1] across methods. Win rate (WR): proportion of perturbations where LCD achieved lower error. (C) Predicted vs. observed mean expression. RMSE over top 20 DE genes (Top) and Pearson correlation of changes relative to perturbed centroid (average of all observed perturbation means) (Bottom). (D) MMD stratified by genetic interaction (GI) type, comparing LCD and the additive baseline SALT. Axis labels indicate significant improvement per GI category (percentage reduction in median MMD by LCD) or not (n.s.; one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, P<0.05). (E) Predicted vs. observed expression for top 20 DE genes of a held-out perturbation with neomorphic GI. Gray section shows the perturbed genes (bold labels). All box plots show the median, interquartile range (IQR), and whiskers extend to farthest points within 1.5× IQR.
figures.attribution: Lars Lorch; Jiaqi Zhang; Charlotte Bunne; Andreas Krause; Bernhard Schölkopf; Caroline Uhler. Latent causal diffusions for single-cell perturbation modeling.. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2602630123. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.

figures.label: Fig. 3.
figures.caption: LCD-CLIPR accurately recovers causal effects in linear systems from learned diffusion drifts. (A) AUROC for classifying gene–gene causal effects (positive, negative, or absent) across all gene pairs. Results are shown for systems of 100, 300, and 1,000 genes across varying training perturbation counts (x-axis), comparing power-law (Left) and Erdős-Rényi (Right) regulatory dependencies in A. (B) F1 score for classifying gene–gene causal effects (Left) and average Pearson correlation between predicted and true causal effects (Right) for the top k predicted effects, ranked by absolute magnitude, under power-law dependencies. Markers indicate medians, error bars indicate 10 to 90th percentiles across test systems. (C) Comparison of causal effects inferred by LCD-CLIPR vs. the ground-truth data-generating system (300 genes). (D) Inferred and true perturbation vectors for the system shown in (C). For visual clarity, only 80 perturbations and 150 genes with the largest outgoing effects are displayed.
figures.attribution: Lars Lorch; Jiaqi Zhang; Charlotte Bunne; Andreas Krause; Bernhard Schölkopf; Caroline Uhler. Latent causal diffusions for single-cell perturbation modeling.. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2602630123. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.

figures.label: Fig. 4.
figures.caption: LCD-CLIPR infers direct gene–gene causal effects from genome-wide Perturb-seq data. (A) Hierarchical clustering based on shortest-path distances in the CLIPR graph identifies gene modules enriched for specific Gene Ontology terms (Top) and canonical pathways (Bottom). Clusters with at least one enriched term are shown. (B) Predicted causal effects and associated clusters from the enrichment analysis. (C) Comparison between observed differential expression (DE) (Left) and normalized L⊤ (Right). For visual clarity, only the 247 genes within identified clusters and their perturbations are shown; see SI Appendix, Figs. S9 and S10 for full matrices. (D) Strongest predicted causal effects (50 total). Gene colors correspond to clusters indicated in (B). Edges are green where the predicted effect is validated by observed DE, and red otherwise. (E and F) Validation of inferred causal links as a function of predicted effect strength. Predicted direct causation (C) significantly increases the probability of observing DE (one-sided Fisher’s exact test, P<0.01, OR: odds ratio). Results shown for all genes (Left) and held-out genes not perturbed during training (Right). Error bars indicate 95% CIs [Wilson binomial for (E), bootstrap for (F)]. Gray dashed lines show the dataset-wide differential expression rate p(DE) (E) and baseline corresponding to independence (F).

ai.title_zh: 面向单细胞扰动建模的潜因果扩散模型
ai.summary_zh: 该文提出潜因果扩散(LCD)生成模型,将单细胞基因表达视为在测量噪声下观测到的平稳扩散过程,并据此学习基因调控的动力学系统;同时提出通过扰动响应进行因果线性化(CLIPR),在漂移线性假设下近似所有基因间的直接因果效应。摘要称 LCD 在预测未见扰动组合的分布偏移上优于已有方法,CLIPR 在模拟系统与全基因组扰动筛选中恢复因果结构。提供的证据仅包含图注与脚本静态观察,作者代码未执行,因此不能确认复现结果。
learning_points: LCD 将单细胞表达 y 建模为未观测无噪声状态 x 的含噪观测,x 由因果调控动力学 f 驱动的随机微分方程生成(Fig. 1A)。
训练分两步:先通过经验贝叶斯推断 p(x),再在状态空间用得分匹配学习 f(Fig. 1A)。
动力学 f 由跨基因共享隐藏状态的神经网络参数化,扰动通过学习的嵌入修改该隐藏状态(Fig. 1B)。
CLIPR 通过扰动下 f 的初始响应与极限响应估计线性因果矩阵,极限响应以沿向量场流至收敛来近似(Fig. 1C)。
Fig. 2 以 MMD、RMSE 与相对扰动质心的变化相关性等指标比较 LCD 与深度学习基线在留出双基因扰动上的预测表现。
Fig. 3 在线性系统中以 AUROC、F1 及预测与真实因果效应的相关性评估 LCD-CLIPR 的因果恢复能力。
Fig. 4 在全基因组 Perturb-seq 数据上基于 CLIPR 图的最短路径距离聚类基因模块,并用观测差异表达检验预测因果链接。

(A) Raw contact maps and (B) corresponding MFPT matrices for chromosome 6 from the GM12878 dataset at the indicated downsampling rates. All matrices are shown at 10‐kb resolution. figures.caption: STRIDE provides consistent and robust library similarity measurements across sequencing depths. (A) Dissimilarity scores among pseudo‐replicates (PR), biological replicates (BR), and non‐replicates (NR) calculated by STRIDE, HiCRep, HiC‐spector, and genomeDISCO at the indicated down‐sampling levels. ai.title_zh: OT-knn:面向空间转录组数据对齐的邻域感知最优传输框架
ai.summary_zh: 该资料介绍 OT-knn,一种在最优传输框架内整合局部邻域信息的空间转录组切片对齐方法:先用每个 spot 的空间 k 近邻做距离加权平均重建其表达谱,再据此计算切片间的概率对应并提取最佳匹配对。图注显示其在模拟扰动、人 DLPFC、小鼠脑衰老、蝾螈脑多阶段及跨平台小鼠胚胎等场景中与 PASTE、DeST-OT、SLAT、Spateo 比较。作者代码未运行,仅作静态观察,未验证复现。
learning_points: 方法流程可拆为五步:选共享高变基因、构建空间 kNN 图、邻域加权重建表达、最优传输求概率对齐、提取最佳匹配对(Fig 1)。
核心思想是用空间邻域上下文替代单 spot 表达,以提升对噪声和变异的稳健性(摘要、Fig 1)。
模拟评估使用已知真值的受控扰动,报告最佳匹配准确率与映射概率准确率(Fig 2)。
真实数据评估覆盖人 DLPFC(Visium)、小鼠脑衰老(MERFISH,含同供体与跨供体)、蝾螈脑(Stereo-seq)及跨平台小鼠胚胎(Fig 3、Fig 4、摘要)。
Fig 3F 展示了最近邻数量对映射概率准确率与最佳匹配准确率的影响,提示 k 为可调超参数。
对比基线包括 PASTE、DeST-OT、SLAT、Spateo,评价指标含最佳匹配准确率、映射概率准确率与域推断结果。
代码仓库存在 OT_knn/__init__.py、data_process.py、OT_knn.py 与 setup.py 等文件,但仅做静态观察,未执行。

figures.label: FIGURE 1
figures.caption: Single‐cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses reveal B‐cell functional reprogramming and proportional imbalance during OA progression and joint aging. (A) Schematic overview of the study design and analytical workflow. Twenty‐four knee‐joint samples (three mice per group) from wild‐type controls, naturally aged mice, and mice at 2, 4, 8, 12, or 24 weeks after OA induction were analyzed by scRNA‐seq. One additional control section and one OA‐24 W section were analyzed by spatial transcriptomics. (B) UMAP visualization of 246,877 cells annotated as Granulocyte‐like cluster 1, B cells, chondrocytes, Granulocyte‐like cluster 2, T cells, erythrocytes, macrophages, or monocytes. (C) Heatmap of representative marker‐gene expression across the annotated populations. (D) Spatial annotation of skeletal muscle/soft tissue, bone, synovium, meniscus, bone marrow, growth plate, cartilage, and subchondral bone. (E) Cell‐type proportions across individual scRNA‐seq samples. Each bar represents one individual mouse; red dashed outlines indicate the B‐cell fraction. (F) UMAP projections showing changes in major populations across OA progression and aging. Red dashed circles highlight B‐cell‐enriched regions; purple dashed circles highlight aging‐associated redistribution. (G) B‐cell proportions across Control, OA‐progression, and aged groups (n = 3 mice per group). Each point represents the B‐cell proportion from one individual mouse. (H) Representative H&E, Safranin O/Fast Green, and FN1/Cd79a immunofluorescence images from 30 M, control, and OA‐24 W joints. Scale bars: 200 µm (histology) and 100 µm (immunofluorescence). (I) Quantification of Cd79a‐positive area in the synovium (ST), subchondral bone (SB), and bone marrow (BM). Each point represents one individual mouse (n = 9 mice per group). Multiple microscopic fields within each anatomical compartment were averaged to obtain one mouse‐level value. * p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; *** p < 0.001; **** p < 0.0001; NS, not significant. (J) Spatial Cd79a expression in control and OA‐24 W sections. Colored spots indicate normalized expression; warmer colors indicate higher values. (K) GO and KEGG enrichment of B‐cell differentially expressed genes. Bar length indicates gene count, and color intensity indicates p value. (L) Representative GSEA plots for IL‐6–JAK–STAT3 signaling, TNF‐α signaling via NF‐κB, glycolysis, and oxidative phosphorylation.

figures.label: FIGURE 2
figures.caption: B cells shift toward senescence‐associated states with concomitant chondrocyte degeneration in OA and aged joints. (A) t‐SNE visualization of B‐cell subtypes identified in mouse joint tissues. (B) Heatmap of representative marker‐gene expression across the annotated B‐cell subtypes. (C) Complete nine‐gene senescence‐associated transcriptional gene set used for AUCell scoring. Genes are grouped according to their biological associations with cell‐cycle arrest, p53/DNA‐damage responses, and senescence‐associated cellular phenotypes. (D) Spatial visualization of senescence AUCell scores in control and OA‐24 W knee sections. Colored spots indicate scores; warmer colors indicate higher values. (E) AUCell scores projected onto t‐SNE embeddings of B cells from 30 M, control, and OA‐24 W groups. (F) KEGG enrichment analysis of B‐cell differentially expressed genes. (G) GO enrichment analysis of B‐cell differentially expressed genes. (H) GSEA plots showing representative pathways in B cell. (I) Pseudotime trajectory showing three inferred B‐cell states and the selected direction from State 2 through State 3 toward State 1. (J) Pseudotime expression dynamics of representative cell‐cycle‐ and proliferation‐associated genes, including Ccna2, Mki67, Pcna, Top2a, and Hmgb1. (K) Heatmap of transcription factors and selected genes dynamically regulated along the B‐cell trajectory. (L) Distribution of B‐cell states across control, OA‐progression, and aged groups. (M) Representative MMP13 and HMGB1 immunofluorescence in 30 M, control, and OA‐24 W joints. Scale bar: 100 µm. (N) Representative Cd79a/HMGB1 immunofluorescence in 30 M, control, and OA‐24 W joints. Dashed rectangles indicate regions containing CD79A‐positive B cells. Scale bar: 100 µm. (O–Q) Quantification of MMP13 fluorescence intensity (O), HMGB1‐positive B cells (P), and HMGB1‐positive chondrocytes (Q) (n = 9 mice per group). Each point represents one individual mouse. * p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; *** p < 0.001; **** p < 0.0001; NS, not significant.

figures.label: FIGURE 3
figures.caption: Enhanced MIF signaling is associated with senescence‐associated B‐cell remodeling and predicted B cell–chondrocyte communication in OA and aged joints. (A) Predicted ligand–receptor communication among major joint‐cell populations in 30 M, control, and OA‐24 W groups. Blue rectangles highlight MIF‐related interactions; dot color indicates communication probability. (B) CellChat network‐centrality analysis of MIF signaling showing sender, receiver, mediator, and influencer activity. (C) Spatially predicted MIF‐associated interaction scores for the CD74/CD44 receptor complex in Control and OA‐24 W sections. Purple outlines indicate Cd79a‐positive B‐cell‐associated spots; colored spots indicate mean interaction scores meeting FDR < 0.05. (D) Representative FN1, Cd79a, and MIF immunofluorescence in 30 M, control, and OA‐24 W joints. Scale bar: 50 µm. (E–H) Quantification of MIF fluorescence intensity (E), proportion of MIF‐positive B cells (F), serum MIF concentration (G), and synovial‐fluid MIF concentration (H) (n = 6 mice per group). Each point represents one individual mouse. * p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; *** p < 0.001; **** p < 0.0001; NS, not significant.

figures.caption: MIF deficiency protects against OA progression and B‐cell senescence‐associated cartilage degeneration in vivo. (A) Skeletal staining of WT and Mif−/− mice. (B, C) Body weight and body length in WT and Mif−/− mice (n = 6 per group). * p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; *** p < 0.001; **** p < 0.0001; NS, not significant. AU, arbitrary units. * p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; *** p < 0.001; **** p < 0.0001; NS, not significant. figures.label: FIGURE 5
figures.caption: Senescence‐associated B cells promote MIF‐dependent chondrocyte senescence and degenerative remodeling in vitro. (A) Experimental design. Joint‐derived B cells from Control, OA‐8 W, OA‐24 W, Mif−/− , and 15 M mice were magnetically isolated and co‐cultured with primary chondrocytes in Transwell inserts. MIF neutralization and recombinant‐MIF add‐back were also tested. (B) P16/P21 immunofluorescence and SA‐β‐gal staining of joint‐derived B cells. (C–F) Quantification of B‐cell P21 (C), P16 (D), SA‐β‐gal positivity (E), and MIF secretion (F) (n = 6 mice per group). * p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; *** p < 0.001; **** p < 0.0001; NS, not significant. (G) COL2A1/FN1, MMP13/HMGB1, and P16/P21 immunofluorescence and SA‐β‐gal staining of chondrocytes after B‐cell co‐culture. (H–N) Quantification of chondrocyte FN1 (H), COL2A1 (I), HMGB1 (J), MMP13 (K), P16 (L), P21 (M), and SA‐β‐gal positivity (N) (n = 6 mice per group). * p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; *** p < 0.001; **** p < 0.0001; NS, not significant. (O) MIF neutralization and add‐back experiments. Chondrocytes were co‐cultured with Control B cells, OA‐24 W B cells plus IgG, OA‐24 W B cells plus anti‐MIF antibody, Mif−/− B cells, or Mif−/− B cells plus recombinant MIF. (P–R) Quantification of P16 (P), P21 (Q), and SA‐β‐gal‐positive chondrocytes (R) (n = 6 mice per group). * p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; *** p < 0.001; **** p < 0.0001; NS, not significant.

figures.label: FIGURE 6
figures.caption: Construction and characterization of a dual‐action siMIF microsphere/quercetin hydrogel. (A) Schematic illustration of the senescent B cell–MIF–chondrocyte axis during OA progression. (B) Design of the siMIF microsphere/quercetin hydrogel (SQH). (C) SEM images of empty and siMIF‐loaded PLGA microspheres and microscopy of rhodamine‐labeled microspheres distributed within the hydrogel. (D) Fluorescence micrographs showing siMIF microsphere‐derived signals in close spatial association with phalloidin‐stained chondrocytes, together with MIF immunofluorescence staining in treated chondrocytes. (E) Mean diameters of empty and siMIF‐loaded microspheres from 12 independently prepared microsphere batches per formulation (n = 12 independent batches per group). NS, not significant. (F) Cumulative in vitro release profile of Cy3‐labeled MIF‐siRNA from PLGA microspheres in PBS and FBS at 37°C over 96 h (n = 12 independently prepared microsphere batches). Data are presented as mean ± SD. (G) Quantification of MIF immunofluorescence intensity in (D) (n = 6 chondrocyte donor mice per group). * p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; *** p < 0.001; **** p < 0.0001; NS, not significant. (H) Representative images of different hydrogel formulations, including quercetin hydrogel (QH), siMIF microsphere hydrogel (SH), and siMIF microsphere/quercetin hydrogel (SQH). Hydrogel shape fidelity after UV crosslinking, chondrocyte morphology, siMIF microsphere‐derived fluorescence associated with chondrocytes, and MIF immunofluorescence staining are shown. (I) Temperature‐dependent rheological analysis of the pre‐crosslinked SQH formulation. Storage modulus (G′) and loss modulus (G″) were measured from 15°C to 45°C. Rheological profiles were obtained from 12 independently prepared SQH samples (n = 12) and were treated as descriptive material‐characterization data. (J) Frequency‐sweep rheological analysis of the final UV‐crosslinked SQH at 17°C. Storage and loss moduli were recorded over an angular‐frequency range of 0.1–10 rad/s using 12 independently prepared SQH samples (n = 12). (K) Quantification of MIF immunofluorescence intensity in (H) (n = 6 chondrocyte donor mice per group). * p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; *** p < 0.001; **** p < 0.0001; NS, not significant.

figures.label: FIGURE 1
figures.caption: Mitochondrial‐derived vesicles act as pro‐calcific mediators in valvular calcification. (A) Schematic illustration of the ex vivo hemodynamic simulation system for vesicle collection from human aortic valve leaflets under physiological pulsatile flow conditions. (B) Immunoblot analysis of EV markers (CD9, CD63), mitochondrial outer membrane protein TOM20, and cytoplasmic marker β‐actin (negative control) in EVs isolated from the perfusate of non‐CAVD and CAVD valve leaflets. (C) Nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) showing the size distribution of isolated EVs from nonCAVD and CAVD perfusates. (D and E) Representative nano‐flow cytometry plots (D) and quantification (E) of TOM20‐positive mitochondrial‐derived vesicles (MDVs) in EVs isolated from nonCAVD and CAVD valve perfusates. (F) Schematic illustration of the immunoadsorption‐based MDV enrichment strategy using TOM20‐conjugated magnetic beads. (G) Alizarin Red S staining (scale bar, 200 μm) of naïve recipient hVICs following treatment with MDV preparations enriched from nonCAVD (MDVnonCAVD) or CAVD (MDVCAVD) valve tissues. (H) Immunoblot analysis of RUNX2 (runt‐related transcription factor 2), OPN (osteopontin), and BMP2 (bone morphogenetic protein 2) in recipient hVICs treated with MDVnonCAVD or MDVCAVD. GAPDH served as the loading control. See Figure S1A for densitometric quantification. (I and J) Representative nano‐flow cytometry plots (I) and quantification (J) of TOM20‐positive MDVs in conditioned media from hVICs cultured under control medium (CM) or pro‐osteogenic medium (OM) conditions. (K) Alizarin Red S staining (scale bar, 200 μm) of naïve recipient hVICs following treatment with MDV preparations derived from CM‐ or OM‐cultured hVICs. (L) Immunoblot analysis of RUNX2, OPN, and BMP2 in recipient hVICs treated with MDV CM or MDV OM . GAPDH served as the loading control. See Figure S1E for densitometric quantification. (M) Representative immunofluorescence co‐staining images of TOM20 (green) and PDH (pyruvate dehydrogenase, magenta) in hVICs cultured under CM or OM conditions. Arrows indicate TOM20+/PDH+ vesicular buds contiguous with donut‐shaped mitochondrial structures. Scale bars, 1.2 μm. (N) Three‐dimensional reconstruction of confocal z‐stacks from an OM‐treated hVIC stained for TOM20 (green) and PDH (magenta), showing a closed, donut‐shaped mitochondrial structure with an attached TOM20+/PDH+ vesicular bud. A rotational view of the reconstructed volume is provided in Video S1. (O) Representative TEM images of aortic valve leaflets from nonCAVD and CAVD patients. Lower panels show higher‐magnification views of the boxed regions; a donut‐shaped mitochondrial profile is evident in the lower CAVD panel, whereas no comparable profile is evident in the lower nonCAVD panel. Scale bars, 1 μm (upper panels) and 0.5 μm (lower panels). A multi‐angle rotational view of the corresponding three‐dimensional TEM reconstruction is provided in Video S2. Data are presented as mean ± SEM (n = 6 independent experiments or patients per group). For densitometric quantification, protein expression levels were normalized to the first group. p values were determined by two‐tailed unpaired Student's t‐test.

figures.label: FIGURE 2
figures.caption: Senescence‐associated features and Gas6 upregulation in CAVD. (A) Representative histological images of nonCAVD and CAVD valve sections stained with von Kossa and Alizarin Red S to detect calcium deposition, and modified Masson's trichrome and Picrosirius Red to assess collagen deposition and fibrotic remodeling. Scale bars, 500 μm. (B, C) Representative immunoblots (B) and densitometric quantification (C) of p16INK4A and p21 protein expression in nonCAVD and CAVD human valve tissues. GAPDH served as the loading control. (D) Representative low‐ and high‐magnification senescence‐associated β‐galactosidase (SA‐β‐gal) staining images of nonCAVD and CAVD human valve tissues. Scale bars, 500 μm (left) and 20 μm (right). (E–G) Representative immunofluorescence co‐staining images of p16INK4A (green) and RUNX2 (magenta) (E), and p21 (green) and RUNX2 (magenta) (F), together with quantification of median nuclear p16INK4A and p21 fluorescence intensity (G), in human non‐CAVD and CAVD valve leaflets. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (blue). Scale bars, 50 μm. (H and I) Representative immunoblots (H) and densitometric quantification (I) of p16INK4A and p21 protein expression in hVICs cultured in control medium (CM) or pro‐osteogenic medium (OM). GAPDH served as the loading control. (J) Representative SA‐β‐gal staining images of CM‐ and OM‐treated hVICs. Lower panels show higher‐magnification views. Scale bar, 200 μm (lower panels). (K) Schematic overview of the multi‐omics screening strategy and subsequent molecular validation using human nonCAVD and CAVD valve tissues. (L) Venn diagram integrating iTRAQ (isobaric tags for relative and absolute quantitation)‐based proteomics and bulk RNA transcriptomics, illustrating the intersection of differentially upregulated proteins (DEP‐UP) and genes (DEG‐UP) and identifying 36 consistently upregulated candidates, including Gas6. (M, N) Representative immunoblots (M) and densitometric quantification (N) of Gas6 and RUNX2 protein expression in nonCAVD and CAVD valve tissues. GAPDH served as the loading control. (O and P) Representative immunofluorescence co‐staining images (O) and quantitative analysis of mean fluorescence intensity (P) for Gas6 (red) and RUNX2 (green) in human nonCAVD and CAVD valve leaflets. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (blue). Scale bar, 50 μm. Data are presented as mean ± SEM (n = 6 per group for human tissue analyzes; n = 6 independent experiments for hVIC analyzes). For densitometric quantification, protein expression levels were normalized to the first group. p16INK4A and p21 immunofluorescence data are expressed as median nuclear fluorescence intensity; Gas6 and RUNX2 immunofluorescence data are expressed as mean fluorescence intensity and normalized to the first group. p values for all quantified between‐group comparisons were determined by two‐tailed unpaired Student's t‐test.

figures.label: FIGURE 4
figures.caption: Gas6 depletion impairs MDV release by inducing a terminal scission defect. (A, B) Representative nano‐flow cytometry plots (A) and quantification (B) of MDVs in conditioned media from hVICs transfected with non‐targeting control siRNA (siCtrl) or Gas6‐targeting siRNA (siGas6) under OM conditions. (C) GSEA of the “Mitochondrial Fission” gene set from MitoCarta3.0 in siGas6 versus siCtrl hVICs under OM conditions. (D–G) Live‐cell imaging, time‐resolved three‐dimensional reconstruction, and quantification of donut‐shaped mitochondria in siCtrl and siGas6 hVICs under OM conditions. (D) Time‐lapse montage showing mitochondrial curling and self‐fusion to form donut‐shaped structures in siGas6 hVICs. Time stamps indicate seconds. Scale bar, 1 μm. See also Video S3. (E) Three selected time points from the time‐resolved three‐dimensional reconstruction of the same mitochondrial‐curling event shown in (D). The continuous reconstruction is provided in Video S4. (F) Representative live‐cell images and (G) quantification of the proportion of donut‐shaped mitochondria in siCtrl and siGas6 hVICs. Scale bars, 30 μm (overview) and 2 μm (inset). (H–L) Time‐lapse imaging, time‐resolved three‐dimensional reconstructions, and quantification of MDV budding dynamics and per‐mitochondrion MDV release. (H) Time‐lapse imaging of siCtrl OM cells showing active MDV budding and membrane detachment. See also Video S5. (I) Three selected time points from the time‐resolved three‐dimensional reconstruction of the same terminal MDV detachment/release event shown in (H). White arrows highlight the terminal budding and detachment sequence. (J) Time‐lapse imaging of siGas6 OM cells demonstrating the “stalled budding” phenotype, with nascent MDVs remaining tethered to parent mitochondria by elongated necks. See also Video S6. Scale bars in (H) and (J), 1 μm. (K) Three selected time points from the time‐resolved three‐dimensional reconstruction of the same stalled‐budding event shown in (J), with the nascent MDV remaining tethered to the parent mitochondrion at the final selected time point. The continuous reconstructions corresponding to (I) and (K) are provided side by side in Video S7. (L) Quantification of MDVs released per mitochondrion. Data are presented as mean ± SEM (n = 6 independent experiments). p values were determined by one‐way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test.

ai.summary_zh: 该资料介绍 CoexpressDeconvolve,一个无需外部单细胞参考的解卷积框架,结合管家基因文库大小校准与空间基因共表达流形上的主题建模,用于从斑点式空间转录组数据恢复整数细胞计数和细胞类型特异转录组。摘要称其在合成 Visium 数据上与 Tangram、cell2location、STdeconvolve 比较,表达重建保真度具竞争力、细胞计数误差最低、每切片细胞类型一致性最高,并输出可载入标准单细胞下游流程的 feature-barcode 矩阵;还应用于人乳腺癌与舌鳞状细胞癌。图 1 展示用于基准测试的乳腺癌 scRNA-seq 图谱,图 2 展示合成 Visium 数据上的表达重建基准,图 3 展示细胞计数与细胞类型比例基准。作者代码未运行,静态检查仅见若干 CSV/TSV 读取片段,不构成复现验证。

关注输出形式差异:摘要强调恢复整数细胞计数与细胞类型特异转录组,而非仅细胞类型比例。

图 2 展示合成 Visium 数据上四种方法的逐细胞类型 Pearson 相关比较,基于 3,000 个高变基因。
图 3 展示每斑点总细胞计数预测与真值的二维密度比较,以及各方法细胞类型比例 RMSE。
摘要称输出 feature-barcode 矩阵可模拟 Space Ranger 输出并载入标准单细胞分析流程。

figures.label: FIGURE 1
figures.caption: Proposed biological mechanisms linking Vitamin D status with Type 2 diabetes pathophysiology. Vitamin D, measured as serum 25‐hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D], is hydroxylated to the active hormone 1,25‐dihydroxyvitamin D [1,25(OH)2D, calcitriol], which is the principal ligand for the Vitamin D receptor (VDR); 25(OH)D itself is the circulating status biomarker rather than the direct VDR ligand. Through 1,25(OH)2D‐mediated VDR signalling and other pathways, Vitamin D status may influence glucose metabolism via three major biological mechanisms: activation of VDR in pancreatic beta cells, leading to improved insulin synthesis and secretion; enhancement of peripheral insulin sensitivity in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue through improved insulin signalling and glucose uptake; and reduction of systemic inflammation through modulation of immune‐cell activity and suppression of pro‐inflammatory cytokines. Together, these mechanisms suggest that Vitamin D may contribute to beta‐cell preservation, improved glucose homeostasis, and reduced inflammatory burden relevant to Type 2 diabetes development and progression. 25(OH)D, 25‐hydroxyvitamin D; CRP, C‐reactive protein; GLUT4, glucose transporter Type 4; IL‐1β, interleukin‐1 beta; IL‐6, interleukin‐6; NF‐κB, nuclear factor kappa B; T2D, Type 2 diabetes; TNF‐α, tumour necrosis factor‐alpha; VDR, Vitamin D receptor.

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.caption: Large-scale evaluation of prokaryotic annotation tools across thousands of species. The Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB 207.0) was queried for representative Bacteria and Archaea species and all Escherichia coli strains. Additionally, genomes were generated from the representatives to include frameshifts of 0.5%, 1%, and 2%. All genomes were annotated using Prokka, Bakta, EggNOG-mapper, and PGAP with their recommended settings. The annotation quality between tools and genome conditions was compared based on multiple characteristics like coding density, detected feature length, Genome Ontology (GO) richness, and impact of frameshifts. Created in BioRender. Röll, D. (2026) biorender.com/2ufrc7z

figures.caption: E. coli coding density and gene length distribution. a Coding density: The average coding density detected by the tools is categorized into described coding density (yellow), undescribed coding density (red), and non-coding regions (gray). Each square represents 1% of the total genome. The mean feature count is noted on the left. b Coding length distribution: The average amino acid length distribution of features for described (yellow) and undescribed (red) coding density is shown

figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.caption: Taxonomy performance analysis. a Average coding density detected by each tool, partitioned into described (yellow), undescribed (red), and non-coding (gray) regions for Bacteria and Archaea. Each square represents 1% of the genome. Mean feature counts are shown on the left, with gains or losses relative to the E. coli baseline indicated below each plot. b Performance ranking per individual genome: Bar charts show how often each tool ranked best per species for total coding density, described coding density, and lowest undescribed coding density. Differences from the second-ranked tool were not considered. c Distribution of rRNA counts in complete and incomplete operons across bacterial genomes. The upper panel shows fragmented genomes (> 10 contigs), whereas the lower panel shows less fragmented genomes (< 10 contigs). Complete operons (multiples of three rRNA genes) are shown in red and incomplete operons in gray. Counts above 24 are omitted for clarity. d Comparison of Gene Ontology (GO) term coverage between PGAP and EggNOG-mapper across 26,970 bacterial genomes. Each point represents a genome; the y-axis shows the maximal GO coverage across both tools, and the x-axis the difference in coverage (EggNOG-mapper − PGAP). The red vertical line indicates equal coverage. The marginal density plot (black outline) shows the parameter distributions. Points right of the red line indicate higher PGAP coverage, whereas points left indicate higher EggNOG-mapper coverage. Gray dots denote genomes from families in which PGAP consistently outperformed EggNOG-mapper; colored dots indicate families with at least one genome favoring EggNOG-mapper. Legends report the number of such cases and total genomes per family. Enterobacteriaceae_A denotes a GTDB-recognized cluster with suffixed placeholder names [15, 16]

figures.label: Fig. 4
figures.caption: Impact of bacterial metagenome-assembled genomes (MAG)s and frameshifts on annotation quality. MAGs: a Breakdown of the average coding density detected by each tool, categorized into described coding density (yellow), undescribed coding density (red), and non-coding density (gray). Each square represents 1% of the total genome. The mean feature count is noted on the left. The annotated gain or loss to the E. coli baseline is outlined in colored numbers below each plot (e.g., a yellow −23 means that this tool annotated 23% less described coding density compared to the baseline). b Performance ranking per individual genome: The bar charts highlight the number of times a tool has achieved the best performance in one of the three categories for each species (largest total, largest described, and lowest undescribed coding density). This approach did not account for the performance difference between the best and second-best tools. Frameshifts: The effect of frameshifts on gene annotations was evaluated under three genome-wide deletion conditions (0.5%, 1%, and 2%) in Bacteria. We displayed mean proportion change to the original sequence of (c) retained coding density, d gene count, and e proportion of hypothetical features compared to the mean original value across four annotation tools (Prokka, Bakta, EggNOG-mapper, and PGAP). The total coding density plot (c) also includes expected differences in coding density based on the different deletion proportions

figures.label: Fig. 5
figures.caption: Simplified decision tree for selecting an appropriate annotation strategy. Prokka is generally not recommended; for projects with low resource requirements where feature detection is the priority, we recommend using Bakta light database as per the author of Prokka's recommendation. If functional annotation is required, the online versions of investigated tools are recommended

ai.summary_zh: 该资料为 Alzheimer's & Dementia 期刊论文(DOI:10.1002/alz.71869,标注时间2026-10-01)的图注与代码静态观察记录。图注显示:研究基于 UK Biobank 中具有完整遗传、蛋白质组、代谢组与临床生物标志物数据的 16,215 名参与者,构建包含多基因风险评分、多种生物学衰老指标与组学衰老时钟的堆叠集成模型用于 ADRD 风险预测,并在 TwinGene 中做外部评估;图2展示各单一预测因子的 AUC 森林图,图3展示 PRS 与各衰老指标间的 Pearson 相关矩阵,图4展示 Fine–Gray 竞争风险模型(以死亡为竞争事件)的亚分布风险比。作者代码未运行,仅作静态观察,未验证复现。
learning_points: 图1以流程图形式给出纳入/排除标准,最终分析样本为 UK Biobank 中具有完整遗传、蛋白质组、代谢组和临床生物标志物数据的 16,215 名参与者。
图1B 汇总了数据输入(多基因风险评分、生物学衰老指标、组学衰老时钟)、预处理/质控步骤与堆叠集成建模框架,并说明最终整合框架在 TwinGene 中用可获得的协调预测因子做外部评估,以区分度和风险分层评估性能。
图2以森林图呈现各单一预测因子在单变量模型中的 AUC 及95%置信区间,预测结局为整个随访期内新发 ADRD。
图3以相关矩阵展示 PRS 与 PhenoAge、KDM、HD、FI、TL、ProtAge、MetaboAge 之间的两两 Pearson 相关系数。
图4以森林图呈现完全调整整合模型(Model 5)中各预测因子的亚分布风险比及95%置信区间,采用 Fine–Gray 竞争风险回归并将死亡作为竞争事件。
图注中列出的衰老相关指标包括 FI(衰弱指数)、HD(稳态失调)、KDM(Klemera–Doubal 法)、PhenoAge(表型年龄)、TL(端粒长度)、ProtAge(蛋白质组衰老时钟)、MetaboAge(代谢组衰老时钟)。

figures.label: FIGURE 1
figures.caption: Associations of 23 ageing biomarkers with all‐cause mortality in the LBC1936. Associations of ageing biomarkers with 16‐year all‐cause mortality were estimated by fitting separate Cox proportional hazards models for each biomarker (N = 656–861 individuals; 326–444 deaths). Models were incrementally adjusted for age and sex (circle), lifestyle risk factors (smoking, alcohol consumption and BMI) (triangle) and seven major medical conditions (crosses). Biomarkers positively associated with mortality are shown in pink, and biomarkers negatively associated with mortality are highlighted in green. All negatively associated biomarkers are labelled with a minus sign preceding their name, and their reciprocal hazard ratios (1/HR) are plotted to facilitate comparison of effect sizes. The vertical dotted line indicates a hazard ratio of 1. Circles represent estimated hazard ratios, with error bars showing 95% confidence intervals. p‐values are adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction, and non‐significant associations are shown in grey (p FDR > 0.05). Proteomic organ clocks are indicated in bold. BMI, body mass index; FER, forced expiratory ratio; FEV, forced expiratory volume in 1 s; FVC, forced vital capacity; GMV/IVC, grey matter volume to intracranial volume ratio; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; TBV/ICV, total brain volume to intracranial volume ratio; WMHV/ICV, white matter hyperintensity volume to intracranial volume ratio.
figures.attribution: Maira Pyrgioti; Ines Mesa Eguiagaray; Paul Redmond; Janie Corley; Mark E. Bastin; Maria Valdés Hernández; et al.. Multimodal Ageing Biomarkers and Plasma Proteomic Signatures Associated With All‐Cause Mortality. DOI: 10.1111/acel.70747. Source: NLM PMC OA Cloud. License: CC BY.

figures.label: FIGURE 2
figures.caption: Plasma proteins and biological functions associated with all‐cause mortality in the LBC1936. (A) Cox models were applied to 9703 SomaScan plasma protein targets to test associations with 16‐year all‐cause mortality, with incremental adjustment for age and sex, lifestyle factors (smoking, alcohol and BMI) and seven medical conditions. The number of significant aptamers and unique proteins after Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction is shown. (B) Top 20 plasma proteins associated with all‐cause mortality after adjustment for age and sex (N = 789 individuals; 404 deaths). Hazard ratios and 95% confidence intervals are plotted with incremental adjustment for age and sex (circles), lifestyle factors (triangles) and medical conditions (crosses). Positive associations are shown in pink and negative associations in green. Negatively associated proteins are labelled with a minus sign preceding their name, and their reciprocal hazard ratios (1/HR) are plotted. p‐values are adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction, and non‐significant associations are shown in grey (p FDR > 0.05). (C‐D) Top five positively and negatively enriched Gene Ontology biological processes (C) and Reactome pathways (D) among mortality‐associated proteins identified by Gene Set Enrichment Analysis. The normalised enrichment score (NES) shows the magnitude and direction of pathway enrichment while accounting for differences in gene set size. Top terms were selected using a composite ranking score calculated as |NES| × −log10(PFDR). The colour scale indicates statistical significance on the −log10(p FDR) scale.

figures.label: FIGURE 3
figures.caption: Top 20 plasma protein predictors of all‐cause mortality in the LBC1936. The plot shows the 20 SomaScan 11k plasma proteins with the largest coefficients from a total of 37 proteins selected to predict all‐cause mortality using elastic net‐penalised Cox regression (N = 789 individuals; 404 deaths). The mixing parameter (α) was set to 0.5, and the penalty parameter (λ) was chosen as 0.16 based on the λmin from 5‐fold cross‐validation. Proteins with positive coefficients, indicating higher mortality risk, are shown in pink, while proteins with negative coefficients, indicating lower mortality risk, are shown in green.

figures.caption: Schematic overview of the multi-omic study design and analytical workflow. PBMCs and serum were collected from a cohort of young (< 5 years) and senior (> 9 years) beagles. Samples underwent parallel processing for single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; N = 30), bulk RNA sequencing (N = 39), serum metabolomics (N = 50), and clinical biomarker measurements (N = 39). These multimodal datasets were integrated with external canine and human GWAS data and murine knockout phenotype data (IMPC) to characterize age-associated molecular landscapes. PBMCs, peripheral blood mononuclear cells; IMPC, International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium, GWAS, genome-wide association studies.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Transcriptomics and metabolomics reveal extensive depletion of ether lipids and dysregulation of central carbon metabolism. (A) Dot plots displaying the Log2FC of metabolites within key differentially enriched Metabolon sub-pathways. Red dots indicate significantly accumulated metabolites (FDR < 0.05) in senior canines, blue dots indicate significantly depleted metabolites, and gray dots represent non-significant trends. The plots highlight the accumulation of Tryptophan metabolites and Phosphatidylethanolamines (PE), contrasting with the widespread depletion of Plasmalogens and Lysoplasmalogens. (B) Integrated visualization of the Citrate (TCA) Cycle pathway (cfa00020). Rectangles represent differentially expressed genes (from bulk RNA-seq) and circles represent differentially abundant metabolites. Red indicates upregulation/accumulation in senior dogs and blue indicates downregulation/depletion in senior dogs. The map illustrates a bottleneck in bioenergetics characterized by the accumulation of Citrate and Pyruvate (red circles) concurrent with the broad downregulation of enzymatic machinery (blue rectangles). (C) Integrated visualization of the Sphingolipid Signaling Pathway (cfa04071). Following the same schema as (B), the map depicts the transcriptional upregulation of signaling receptors and kinases (red rectangles) amidst complex shifts in lipid substrates, aligning with the observed remodeling of membrane composition and signaling responsiveness.

figures.label: Fig. 1
figures.caption: A framework for modeling cellular aging with plasma proteomics.a, Study design for evaluating plasma proteomic signatures of cellular aging across platforms and cohorts: plasma proteins were mapped to cell types using the Human Protein Atlas, cell type-enriched proteins were used to train machine learning models that predict chronological age, cell type-specific age gaps were calculated and z-scored to enable comparisons across cell types, cross-platform validation was performed in three independent cohorts: the GNPC (n = 14,281, SomaScan), the UKB (n = 44,458, Olink) and the 1946 NSHD (n = 1,803, SomaScan), cellular age gaps were quantified and used to describe heterogeneous aging patterns, predict disease risk and stratify survival outcomes. b, Plasma protein expression trajectories for six illustrative cell types in healthy individuals in the GNPC cohort (n = 7,074). Trajectories were modeled using LOWESS regression for individuals aged 20 to 90 years, with each plot showing proteins assigned to the indicated cell type. c, Illustrative cellular aging models trained on healthy individuals in the Knight-ADRC cohort (n = 1,398). Scatter plots show estimated biological age versus chronological age with corresponding correlation coefficients (r). Bar plots display mean coefficients (±s.d.) of the top proteins by magnitude in each cellular aging model. Illustrations in a created in BioRender; Augustina, V. https://biorender.com/7k7rct4 (2026).

figures.label: Fig. 2
figures.caption: Cellular aging signatures reveal individual heterogeneity.a, Age-dependent patterns of extreme cellular aging in healthy individuals within the GNPC cohort (n = 7,074). Heatmap shows the percentage of extreme agers across 43 cell types (columns) and five chronological age windows (rows), with extreme agers defined as individuals with age gap at least two s.d. from the mean. b, Cellular aging and modifiable risk factors in the UKB cohort. Representative cellular aging profiles for individuals with a healthy lifestyle (left: n = 1,044) defined as never smoking, no regular alcohol consumption, at least 5 days per week of 10+ min of moderate or vigorous physical activity, BMI < 25, waist circumference <90 cm for men or <84 cm for women, ≥7 h of sleep nightly, and individuals with concurrent smoking and obesity (right: n = 1,046). Color intensity corresponds to the mean z-scored age gap. c, Bar plots show mean z-scored age gaps for astrocytes (left) and macrophages (right) stratified by APOE genotype (APOE2/2: n = 369, APOE2/3: n = 5,202, APOE3/3: n = 24,841, APOE3/4: n = 10,059, APOE4/4: n = 1,267) in the UKB cohort. Data are presented with error bars indicating 95% CI. Statistical significance between APOE genotype groups was assessed using two-sided independent t-tests. P values are indicated as *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01 and ***P < 0.001. d, Correlation network showing cellular aging patterns across cell types in healthy individuals in the GNPC cohort (n = 7,074). Each node represents a specific cell type, with two nodes connected if the correlation of age gaps between the two cell types is above a threshold of 0.35. Edge width corresponds to correlation strength, with edges highlighting the top 15 correlations. e, Stability of extreme cellular aging over a 10-year period for individuals categorized as macrophage extreme agers (top: n = 9, z-scored age gap >2) and alveolar type 2 cell extreme agers (bottom: n = 11, z-scored age gap >2) in the NSHD cohort (timepoints: 63.2 ± 1.1 years (baseline), 70.7 ± 0.7 years (visit 2), 72.9 ± 0.6 years (visit 3), n = 364 across all timepoints). Age ranges are represented as mean ± s.d years. Bars show the proportion of extreme old, extreme young and normal agers at each timepoint, with extreme groups proportionally scaled for visualization. figures.label: Fig. 3
figures.caption: Cell type-specific age estimates are associated with neurodegenerative diseases.a, Correlation between cell type-specific age gaps and neurodegenerative disease diagnosis in the GNPC cohort. Analysis includes AD (n = 2,761), ALS (n = 245), PD (n = 476), FTD (n = 199) and MCI–SCI (n = 1,992). Associations with adjusted P values below 0.01 and correlation magnitudes greater than 0.05 are shown in color, with color intensity corresponding to correlation strength, and significance levels annotated. Associations between continuous cellular age gaps and binary disease status were assessed using two-sided point-biserial correlation, with P values adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (*P < 0.01, **P < 0.001 and ***P < 0.0001). b, Estimated biological age of skeletal myocytes (left) and cardiomyocytes (right) versus chronological age by neurodegenerative disease diagnosis in the GNPC cohort. Each dot represents an individual, colored by disease diagnosis. A locally weighted scatterplot smoothing (LOWESS) regression fit was used to estimate the relationship between estimated biological and chronological age for each group. c, Cumulative incidence of ALS over 15 years of follow-up in the UKB cohort, stratified by skeletal myocyte (left) and cardiomyocyte (right) aging status. Extreme, normal and youthful agers are shown, with sample sizes in the legend. Lines represent Kaplan–Meier estimates, and shaded bands indicate 95% CIs. Overall log-rank test comparing cumulative incidence across youthful, normal and extreme ager groups: skeletal myocyte aging, P < 0.0001, cardiomyocyte aging: P = 0.0562. d, AD cumulative incidence by astrocyte aging status over 15 years of follow-up in the UKB cohort: extreme agers (n = 1,161), normal agers (n = 41,896) and youthful agers (n = 829). Lines represent Kaplan–Meier estimates of cumulative incidence, and shaded bands indicate 95% CIs. Overall log-rank test comparing cumulative incidence across extreme young, normal and extreme ager groups: P < 0.0001. e, AD cumulative incidence stratified by APOE genotype and astrocyte aging status over 15 years of follow-up in the UKB cohort. Rows: APOE genotype (APOE2/2: n = 364, APOE2/3: n = 5,165, APOE3/3: n = 27,263, APOE3/4: n = 9,884, APOE4/4: n = 1,210). Columns: astrocyte aging (extreme: n = 1,161, normal: n = 41,896, youthful n = 829). Color intensity indicates the cumulative incidence percentage, with numbers displayed in each cell indicating the total number of individuals and the number who developed AD during follow-up. f, HRs with 95% CIs for incident AD by risk factor in the UKB cohort. HRs correspond to exponentiated model coefficients, and horizontal lines denote 95% CIs. Overall and sex-stratified results are shown, with sample sizes indicated below each label. g, AD cumulative incidence by astrocyte aging status across APOE genotypes in the UKB cohort for extreme, normal and youthful agers. Left: APOE3/3: n = 27,263, middle: APOE3/4: n = 9,884, right: APOE4/4: n = 1,210. Lines represent Kaplan–Meier estimates of cumulative incidence, and shaded bands indicate 95% CIs. Within each APOE genotype stratum, group differences were assessed using a two-sided log-rank test comparing the extreme astrocyte aging group with the combined young and normal ager groups: APOE3/3: P < 0.0001, APOE3/4: P < 0.0001, APOE4/4: P < 0.0001. h, Cellular age gap associations with plasma pTau-217 burden (pg ml−1) and PACC (a composite measure of cognitive performance) in the NSHD cohort Insight-46 substudy (n = 483). Associations were assessed using linear regression models adjusted for chronological age and sex. For analyses involving PACC, models were additionally adjusted for childhood cognitive ability to account for baseline differences in cognition. Effect sizes are reported as regression coefficients, with two-sided P values derived from t-statistics and corrected for multiple testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01 and ***P < 0.001). Lower PACC scores indicate worse cognitive performance.

figures.label: Fig. 5
figures.caption: Cellular aging states inform survival and resilience.a, Analysis of cellular aging and all-cause mortality risk over 15 years of follow-up in the UKB cohort. HRs with 95% CI for all-cause mortality are shown, estimated using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for chronological age and sex. Results shown for overall analysis (men and women combined, n = 44,458) and sex-stratified analyses (females: n = 24,046, males: n = 20,412). For each cell type, dark shaded markers represent estimates derived from extreme cellular aging and light shaded markers represent estimates derived from per-unit increase in age gap per cell type and or lineage. HRs correspond to exponentiated model coefficients, and horizontal lines denote 95% CIs. The top 30 cell types with the strongest associations with mortality risk are shown. b, HRs for all-cause mortality by cell type at three timepoints in the NSHD cohort (n = 364; baseline 63.2 ± 1.1 years, timepoint 2: 70.7 ± 0.7 years, timepoint 3: 72.9 ± 0.6 years; followed to a mean age of 78.2 ± 0.3 years). Associations between cell-type age gaps and mortality risk were assessed using Cox proportional hazards models, with time since blood draw as the time scale and death as the event. Models included z-scored age gaps with adjustment for chronological age and sex. Effect sizes are reported as HRs with 95% CIs. Two-sided P values were derived from Wald tests and adjusted using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. The top 25 cell types with strongest associations with mortality risk at the third timepoint are shown. c, Kaplan–Meier survival curves stratified by cellular aging status for muscle lineage (left), neuron lineage (middle) and immune lineage cell types (right) in the UKB cohort. Participants were categorized as extreme old (red; muscle: n = 1,097, neurons: n = 1,437, immune: n = 1,170), normal (green; muscle: n = 42,605, neurons: n = 42,437, immune: n = 42,440) or extreme young (blue; muscle: n = 765, neurons: n = 584, immune: n = 848) based on z-scored lineage and cell type age gaps. Lines represent Kaplan–Meier estimates of survival, and shaded bands indicate 95% CIs. Group differences were assessed using two-sided log-rank tests: muscle lineage, P < 0.0001; neuron lineage, P < 0.0001; immune lineage, P < 0.0001. d, All-cause mortality by number of extreme aging cell types over 15 years of follow-up in the UKB cohort. Kaplan–Meier curves stratified by extreme aging burden: normal agers (n = 10,155, ~90% survival); 1–5 extreme cell types (n = 30,239, ~85%); 6–10 (n = 2,940, ~73%); 11–20 (n = 862, ~52%); 20+ (n = 262, ~34%). Additional curves show individuals with youthful immune lineage (n = 848) or neuron lineage cell types (n = 584) irrespective of other cell-type aging patterns. Lines represent Kaplan–Meier estimates of survival, and shaded bands indicate 95% CIs. e, Polycellular aging risk score (PARS) for mortality stratification across plasma proteomics platforms and independent cohorts. Bar plot shows the top 15 cell-type contributors (model coefficients) for the PARS score. The PARS was derived from a multivariate Cox proportional hazards model trained in the UKB training cohort (n = 21,983). Predictors included binary extreme aging indicators and sex, with model selection performed using 10-fold cross-validation. Positive coefficients denote elevated mortality risk. f, Kaplan–Meier survival curves show risk stratification based on PARS in the UKB training cohort (top) (n = 21,983), UKB test cohort (middle) (n = 22,475) and NSHD validation cohort (bottom) (n = 1,803). Participants were categorized into low (bottom 5%), medium (middle 90%) and high (top 5%) risk groups based on cohort-specific score distributions. Lines represent Kaplan–Meier estimates of survival, and shaded bands indicate 95% CIs. Group differences were assessed using two-sided log-rank tests; with sample sizes and P values indicated in the figure legends.

figures.caption: DNAm and transcriptomic clocks comparing in vivo and in vitro aging. (a) Human fibroblasts of donors aged 0–92 years were harvested once reaching confluency (in vivo aging). RNA‐seq and DNAm EPIC Array were performed at 5–7 time‐points each 30 days. (b) Phase contrast images taken at time of harvest each month. figures.label: FIGURE 2
figures.caption: In vitro aging transcriptome changes are concordant with human fibroblast aging in vivo. (a) Linear regression of gene expression with age. In vivo aging analyses were adjusted for sex (model: Age + sex). The top 100 up‐ and downregulated genes along in vitro aging (green), in vivo aging (blue), and Fleischer et al. in vivo aging (brown) are shown. (b) Schematic of overlapping pathway analysis performed using CLUEGO (Cytoscape). Up‐ and downregulated aging genes were analyzed separately for in vitro aging (adjusted p < 0.05), Fleischer et al. in vivo aging (adjusted p < 0.05), and our in vivo aging dataset (p < 0.05). Gene‐set enrichment analysis was used to determine significance (adjusted p < 0.1; fgsea, R). Venn diagram depicts overlap among significantly enriched pathways. (c, d) Representative accelerated up‐ and downregulated KEGG pathways. Vst‐normalized expression was averaged per pathway, and linear regression was used to estimate pathway‐level slopes. To assess pathway‐level differences between in vitro and in vivo aging at gene‐level, we fit a linear model including an interaction term between age and dataset (Age × Dataset) with in vitro aging as reference. Interaction p‐value was corrected for multiple testing using the Benjamini–Hochberg method. (e) Average slopes of genes contributing to upregulated (n = 7) and downregulated (n = 17) pathways. Each dot representing one pathway; slopes were calculated based on changes in vst‐normalized gene expression per year. For upregulated pathways, data met normality assumptions and were analyzed using Brown‐Forsythe ANOVA (df = 2, p = 0.0017) followed by Dunnett's multiple comparisons test (in vitro vs. in vivo p = 0.009, in vitro vs. Fleischer p < 0.009 in vivo vs. Fleischer p = 0.97). For downregulated pathways, normality assumptions were not met and differences were assessed using Kruskal‐Wallis test (H = 37.71, df = 2, in vitro vs. in vivo p = 0.0002, in vitro vs. Fleischer p < 0.0001, in vivo vs. Fleischer p = 0.11). (f, g) Gene expression (green) and corresponding promoter methylation (orange)—defined as methylation at TSS200, TSS1500, 5′UTR, and 1st exon regions—of genes contributing to upregulated (n = 7) and downregulated (n = 17) aging pathways in in vitro aging. Values were averaged per pathway. Standard deviation represents variance between pathways. (h) iN‐competent fibroblasts (stable UNA expression) were pre‐aged with the established protocol and converted to iNs at baseline (M0) and after 6 months of in vitro aging. (i) Immunofluorescence staining of iN cultures for neuronal markers after 21 days of conversion induction. (j) Conversion efficacy at Day 21 of conversion. Each dot represents an independent donor, based on the average of 2–3 images per donor. TUJ: Paired t‐test (t(3) = 0.74, 95% CI [−20, 32]). MAP2 and NeuN did not meet normality assumption, Wilcoxon test was performed on 4 paired samples (NeuN W = 10, median difference = 13; MAP2 W = 10, median difference = 9). (k–m) Epigenetic and transcriptomic age calculations (n = 3 per time‐point). (k) Blood&Skin DNAm clock. Each dot represents an individual donor. Paired t‐test (t(2) = 4.4, 95% CI [0.1, 8.3]). (l) tAge. Paired t‐test (t(2) = 7.6, 95% CI [2.8, 10.3]). (m) RNAAgeCalculator—brain‐specific. Paired t‐test (t(2) = 49.7, 95% CI [19.6, 23.4]). (n) Subtraction of baseline estimated age from age at month six. Repeated measures ANOVA, F(1, 21, 2.24) = 434.5, p = 0.0013, Tukey's multiple comparisons test. (o) Aging velocity as calculated by simple linear regression per donor (slope). Repeated measures ANOVA, F(1, 25, 2.5) = 565.7, p = 0.0005, Tukey's multiple comparisons test. (e, j–o) Significance: *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001, ****p < 0.0001.

figures.caption: Anti‐aging drug Metformin to slow aging in vitro. (a) Fibroblasts at confluency were treated with Metformin (1 mM) for 6 months (n = 4 independent donors). No overt morphological differences were observed. Cells were harvested each month (30 days) for RNA and DNA extraction to assess DNAm age (Blood&Skin clock) and transcriptomic age (RNAAgeCalc—across‐tissue). (b) Slopes of DNAm Blood&Skin clock in Control (gray) and Metformin‐treated (red) cultures (n = 4/group). Statistical comparison was performed using a mixed linear effect model (treatment × time in vitro: Estimate = −0.18 ± 0.09, t(49) = −2.1). Average simple linear regression slopes across all donors were plotted. (c) Years aged in vitro was calculated by subtracting the age of Month 0 from Month 6 in Control (gray) and Metformin‐treated cultures (red). Paired t‐test was performed (t(3) = 4.4, 95% CI [−20, −3], p = 0.02). (d) Mixed‐effects linear model was performed. Gray bars represent baseline slope of linear regression with time in vitro (as years, vst‐normalized), red bars represent the treatment slope. A red slope of 0 indicates that Metformin fully (100%) rescues the aging pathway, and is no longer up‐ or downregulated. For each pathway, gene‐wise baseline slopes and treatment interaction slopes were extracted and compared using paired t‐test (adjusted for multiple testing, FDR). figures.label: FIGURE 1
figures.caption: Overview of the CAPER framework. (A) CAPER is a statistical matrix‐factorization framework designed to disentangle true biological signals from unwanted technical and sample‐to‐sample variation. The method takes as input scaled, normalized gene expression matrices from single‐cell experiments spanning multiple conditions. Through its factorization approach, CAPER explicitly separates biological states from condition‐specific variations, outputting two key products: (1) interpretable latent factors that capture shared cell‐state structure and reproducible condition‐associated biological effects, and (2) a corrected gene expression matrix in which the signal of interest is preserved and isolated for robust downstream analysis. (B) The schematic illustrates CAPER's ability to recover biological structure across different signal‐to‐noise regimes: (1) High SNR; (2) Confounded SNR; (3) Low SNR. In the UMAP embedding, weakly responsive cell populations remain nearly overlapped between conditions, moderately responsive populations remain partially overlapped, and strongly responsive populations become nearly separated.

figures.label: FIGURE 2
figures.caption: Benchmarking CAPER in simulations across different signal‐to‐noise ratio settings. (A) UMAP visualization of the uncorrected raw simulated data in the high‐SNR scenario. Cells are colored by condition and cell population, showing that the condition‐associated signal is stronger than noise before correction. (B) Quantitative benchmark in the high‐SNR scenario. The bubble plot summarizes the total score, biological conservation metrics, and batch‐correction metrics across methods, showing that CAPER achieves the highest total score while maintaining a favorable balance between biological conservation and batch correction. (C) UMAP visualization of corrected simulated data in the high‐SNR scenario. UMAP plots show cells colored by condition and cell population, demonstrating that CAPER preserves cell‐population structure and condition‐associated biological signal while reducing unwanted variation. (D) UMAP visualization of the uncorrected raw simulated data in the confounded‐SNR scenario. Cells are colored by condition and cell population, showing that the condition‐associated signal is comparable to noise before correction. (E) Quantitative benchmark in the confounded‐SNR scenario. The bubble plot summarizes benchmark metrics across methods, showing that CAPER achieves the highest total score and maintains a favorable balance between biological conservation and batch correction. (F) UMAP visualization of corrected simulated data in the confounded‐SNR scenario. UMAP plots show cells colored by condition and cell population, demonstrating that CAPER maintains cell‐population organization under stronger confounding. (G) UMAP visualization of the uncorrected raw simulated data in the low‐SNR scenario. Cells are colored by condition and cell population, showing that the condition‐associated signal is weaker than noise before correction. (H) Quantitative benchmark in the low‐SNR scenario. The bubble plot summarizes benchmark metrics across methods, showing that CAPER achieves the highest total score and maintains strong biological conservation and batch‐correction performance. (I) UMAP visualization of corrected simulated data in the low‐SNR scenario. UMAP plots show cells colored by condition and cell population, demonstrating that CAPER preserves cell‐population structure even when condition‐associated signals are weak.

figures.label: FIGURE 3
figures.caption: CAPER identifies cell populations and genes responsive to the interferon‐β stimulation. (A) Experimental design of the PBMC dataset. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were collected from eight patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The dataset comprises 7466 cells from the IFN‐β‐stimulated condition (stimulated) and 6573 cells from matched control samples, enabling direct comparison of perturbation responses across cell types. (B) UMAP visualization of corrected PBMC data. The gene expression matrices reconstructed by CAPER, CellANOVA, scDisInFact, scVI, scGen, ComBat, fastMNN, and uncorrected Raw were projected into 2D UMAP embeddings. Cells are colored by condition (top row) and annotated cell type (bottom row), demonstrating that CAPER preserves major cell‐population structure while retaining IFN‐β‐associated transcriptional differences in responsive populations. (C) Quantitative benchmark of PBMC data integration. The benchmark summary compares overall performance, biological conservation, and batch correction metrics across methods, showing that CAPER achieves the highest total score and the strongest biological conservation. (D) Perturbation response intensity across cell types. Bar plots show the number of overlapping genes between the top 50 upregulated differentially expressed (DE) genes per cell type and a reference set of interferon‐stimulated genes (ISGs) from the Interferome database. CAPER identifies CD14+ monocytes, FCGR3A+ monocytes, and dendritic cells as strongly responsive populations. scDisInFact fails to distinguish perturbation intensity across cell types, yielding uniformly high overlap. (E) Top contributing genes to major axes of variation. Lollipop plots display the top 10 genes with the most positive and most negative loadings on the first three principal components (PCs) identified by CAPER. These genes represent the primary sources of biological variation captured by CAPER. (F) Top contributing genes to major axes of variation. Lollipop plots display the top ten genes with the most positive and most negative loadings on the first three principal components (PCs) identified by CellANOVA. These genes represent the primary sources of biological variation captured by CellANOVA. (G) Corrected expression of representative genes in CD14+ monocytes. Violin plots show expression of IFI44L and UTRN across stimulated and control cells, demonstrating that CAPER recovers the expected upregulation of the interferon‐stimulated gene IFI44L while avoiding a biologically unsupported DE call for UTRN. (H) Overlap of GO terms enriched by upregulated DE genes across methods in CD14+ monocyte. The UpSet plot summarizes shared and method‐specific GO terms enriched by upregulated DE genes across CAPER and compared methods. (I) Interferon‐response pathway recovery in CD14+ monocytes. The heatmap summarizes keyword‐matched interferon‐ and immune‐response GO terms enriched among upregulated DE genes, showing stronger pathway‐level recovery by CAPER. (J) Co‐expression module eigengene analysis. Violin plots show stimulated‐control differences in representative co‐expression module eigengenes, indicating that CAPER‐corrected expression supports co‐expression analysis. (K) Hub‐gene networks of co‐expression modules. Network plots show representative hub genes from CAPER‐derived modules, including interferon‐stimulated genes such as IFIT3, CXCL10, and ISG15, and inflammatory chemokine‐related genes such as CCL23, CCL4, and CCL3.

figures.label: FIGURE 4
figures.caption: CAPER identifies LUAD‐associated cell populations and genes. (A) Experimental design of the LUAD dataset. The dataset includes 27 509 cells from eight tumor samples and 36 381 cells from eleven paracancerous control samples, enabling analysis of tumor‐associated transcriptional changes in a confounded‐SNR setting. (B) UMAP visualization of corrected LUAD data. The gene expression matrices reconstructed by CAPER, CellANOVA, scDisInFact, scVI, scGen, ComBat, fastMNN, and uncorrected Raw were projected into 2D UMAP embeddings. Cells are colored by condition (tumor vs. control; top row) and annotated cell type (bottom row), demonstrating that CAPER preserves major cell‐population structure while retaining tumor‐control transcriptional differences in LUAD‐relevant populations. (C) Quantitative benchmark of LUAD data integration. The benchmark summary compares overall performance, biological conservation, and batch correction metrics, showing that CAPER achieves the highest total score and strongest biological conservation. (D) Perturbation response intensity across cell populations. Lollipop plots display the mean area under the ROC curve (AUC) from Augur analysis for each cell type, quantifying the responsiveness of each population to tumor‐associated changes. CAPER identifies the strongest responses in epithelial cells, which are known to play critical roles in LUAD pathogenesis. ComBat fails to distinguish response intensity across cell types, yielding uniformly high or flat signals. (E) Top contributing genes to major axes of variation. Lollipop plots display the top ten genes with the most positive and most negative loadings on the first three principal components identified by CAPER. These genes represent the primary sources of tumor‐associated biological variation captured by CAPER. (F) Top contributing genes to major axes of variation. Lollipop plots display the top ten genes with the most positive and most negative loadings on the first three principal components identified by CellANOVA. These genes represent the primary sources of tumor‐associated biological variation captured by CellANOVA. (G) Corrected expression of representative genes in epithelial cells. Violin plots show expression of UBE2S and IFT27 across tumor and control cells, demonstrating that CAPER recovers tumor‐associated upregulation of UBE2S while avoiding a statistically unsupported DE call for IFT27. (H) Overlap of upregulated DE genes in epithelial cells. The UpSet plot summarizes shared and method‐specific upregulated DE genes across CAPER and compared methods. (I) Functional enrichment of method‐specific upregulated DE genes. Bubble plots show enriched GO terms among method‐specific upregulated DE genes in epithelial cells, indicating that CAPER‐specific genes are enriched for vascular and angiogenesis‐related pathways. (J) Survival prediction using method‐derived gene signatures. Kaplan‐Meier curves show survival probabilities for low‐risk and high‐risk patient groups stratified by Cox proportional hazards models built from the top 40 DE genes identified by each method, applied to independent TCGA LUAD bulk RNA‐seq data. Shaded areas indicate 95% confidence intervals. Insets display key performance metrics for each model: significant gene ratio (proportion of genes with Wald test p < 0.05), concordance index (C‐index), Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), Brier score, and log‐rank p‐value. The gene signature derived from CAPER's corrected expression matrix significantly stratifies patient survival and achieves competitive predictive performance, including the highest C‐index among the compared methods, suggesting that CAPER‐recovered epithelial signals carry prognostic information.

figures.label: FIGURE 5
figures.caption: CAPER identifies the T1D‐dependent cell populations and genes. (A) Experimental design of the T1D dataset. Pancreatic islet tissues were collected from five patients with type 1 diabetes (T1D) and eleven healthy controls. The dataset comprises 22 400 cells from T1D donors and 26 594 cells from control donors, enabling investigation of disease‐associated transcriptional changes in rare and subtle cell populations. (B) UMAP visualization of corrected T1D data. The gene expression matrices reconstructed by CAPER, CellANOVA, scDisInFact, scVI, scGen, ComBat, fastMNN, and uncorrected Raw were projected into 2D UMAP embeddings. Cells are colored by condition (T1D vs. control; top row) and annotated cell type (bottom row). CAPER preserves subtle separation between T1D and control cells in disease‐relevant populations while maintaining overall biological structure. (C) Quantitative benchmark of T1D data integration. The benchmark summary compares overall performance, biological conservation, and batch correction metrics, showing that CAPER achieves the highest total score across methods. (D) Perturbation response intensity across cell types. Lollipop plots display the mean area under the ROC curve (AUC) from Augur analysis for each cell type, quantifying the responsiveness of each population to T1D‐associated changes. CAPER and CellANOVA identify the strongest responses in pancreatic A cells and type B pancreatic cells, which are the key cell types implicated in T1D pathogenesis. In contrast, analysis of raw uncorrected data identifies strongest responses in ductal cells, reflecting confounding by sample heterogeneity. scDisInFact produced high Augur scores across multiple endocrine and non‐endocrine populations and ranked pancreatic ductal cells first, suggesting reduced specificity in prioritizing T1D‐relevant endocrine responses. (E) Top contributing genes to major axes of variation. Lollipop plots display the top 10 genes with the most positive and most negative loadings on the first three principal components identified by CAPER. These genes represent the primary sources of T1D‐associated biological variation captured by CAPER. (F) Top contributing genes to major axes of variation. Lollipop plots display the top 10 genes with the most positive and most negative loadings on the first three principal components identified by CellANOVA. These genes represent the primary sources of T1D‐associated biological variation captured by CellANOVA. (G) Corrected expression of representative genes in type B pancreatic cells. Violin plots show expression of NLRP1 and HOOK2 across T1D and control cells, demonstrating that CAPER recovers disease‐associated upregulation of NLRP1 while avoiding a biologically unsupported DE call for HOOK2. (H) Pairwise overlap of DE genes in type B pancreatic cells. Stacked bar plots summarize shared, CAPER‐unique, and compared method‐unique DE genes for each CAPER‐vs.‐compared method comparison. (I) Functional enrichment of CAPER‐unique DE genes. Bubble plots show enriched GO terms among CAPER‐unique DE genes from pairwise comparisons, highlighting β‐cell‐relevant vesicle‐localization, endoplasmic‐reticulum‐stress, and synaptic‐vesicle‐exocytosis programs. (J) Trajectory inference and ROS pathway activity analysis using CAPER‐corrected expression. UMAP plots show type B pancreatic cells colored by condition and diffusion pseudotime, followed by pseudotime comparison between T1D and control cells and ROS pathway activity along pseudotime, indicating a T1D‐associated β‐cell progression pattern linked to oxidative‐stress activation.

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Architecture of the HiCP2GAN plug-and-play adversarial framework for Hi-C resolution enhancement. (A) Generator: A generator-agnostic enhancement module (e.g. HiCARN1, DiCARN, or other compatible architectures) takes low-resolution Hi-C contact matrices as input and produces enhanced Hi-C maps, enabling seamless integration of diverse enhancement models within a unified adversarial framework. (B) HiCFoundation Discriminator: A pretrained transformer-based discriminator initialized from HiCFoundation provides structural priors for chromatin interaction modeling. The discriminator consists of convolutional feature extractors, multi-head self-attention blocks, and feed-forward layers followed by a lightweight GAN head. The deeper transformer layers are frozen to preserve pretrained representations, while the earlier layers (closer to the input) and GAN head are finetuned during adversarial training. Adversarial and feature-matching losses guide generator optimization, enabling resolution enhancement informed by both local convolutional patterns and global chromatin interaction structure.

ai.summary_zh: 该资料介绍HiCP2GAN,一种即插即用的对抗式Hi-C分辨率增强框架:生成器可为任意兼容的增强架构(如HiCARN1、DiCARN等),判别器则初始化自预训练的Vision Transformer型Hi-C基础模型HiCFoundation,其深层transformer层冻结、靠近输入的浅层与轻量GAN头微调,并以对抗损失与特征匹配损失指导生成器优化。图注显示在GM12878测试染色体上集成后loop F1提升,并在K562示例区域展示TAD接触图对比。作者代码未运行,静态检查不构成复现验证。
learning_points: 判别器采用预训练Hi-C基础模型(HiCFoundation)作为骨干,提供染色质结构先验,而非从零训练自定义判别器。
框架生成器无关,可接入HiCARN1、DiCARN等兼容增强模型,便于在统一对抗框架下比较不同方法。
微调策略为冻结深层transformer层、微调靠近输入的浅层及轻量GAN头,以保留预训练表示并做任务适配。
训练目标包含对抗损失与特征匹配损失,兼顾局部卷积模式与全局染色质交互结构。
图2通过不同微调层数的验证PSNR曲线选择判别器配置(100 epochs)。
图3显示在GM12878测试染色体(chr4、chr14、chr16、chr20)上,集成HiCP2GAN的四种生成器loop F1均提升,其中HiCP2GAN-DiCARN最高。
图4以K562 chr14:70–75 Mb单一区域展示独立生成器与HiCP2GAN变体的TAD接触图,并标注TopDom结构域边界。
摘要称判别器在跨物种、跨细胞类型的1.18亿个Hi-C patch上预训练。
limitations: 作者代码未执行,静态检查不是复现验证,不能宣称已复现或与原文结果一致。
输入数据的具体尺度、预处理细节及图号与数据的对应关系在证据中未明示,属未知。
图2仅给出验证PSNR随epoch变化的描述,未提供具体数值或统计检验。
图3仅涉及GM12878四个测试染色体的loop F1,其他细胞系与指标未在证据中展开。
图4仅为K562单一示例区域的定性展示,定量一致性指向Table 6但该表内容未提供。
摘要中“多数设置下优于传统GAN方法”的结论未在所提供的图注证据中给出完整数值支撑。
基础模型预训练数据规模(1.18亿patch)仅来自摘要表述,未在证据中独立核实。
未观察到许可、期刊指标等信息,均属未知。
脚本证据仅记录文件路径与哈希及一处np.loadtxt读取语句,未体现完整绘图流程。
未提供运行环境、超参数与随机种子等信息,可复现性细节未知。
